title: San Francisco: Chinatown, North Beach and Telegraph Hill
summary: Walk from the Dragon Gate through Chinatown's temples and alleys, into the Italian cafés and Beat poetry of North Beach, then climb Telegraph Hill to Coit Tower and one of the best views of the bay.
intro: Welcome to San Francisco! I'm your guide for the next two and a half hours or so. We'll start at the Dragon Gate, walk up through Chinatown, cross into the old Italian neighborhood of North Beach, and finish on top of Telegraph Hill at Coit Tower. Keep your phone screen on and your headphones in. When you reach each place, I'll start talking on my own, and between stops I'll tell you where to turn. Want to hear something again? Just tap it on the map. The first half is flat, but the end is a real climb, so pace yourself and bring some water. Let's go.

stops.name: Dragon Gate
stops.text: You're standing at the Dragon Gate, the main entrance to San Francisco's Chinatown. It opened in 1970, built with help from Taiwan. Look up at the green tiled roofs, the dragons on top, and the two stone lions guarding the way. The four golden characters in the middle are a saying made famous by Sun Yat-sen, the father of modern China. They're usually translated as: all under heaven is for the people. Chinese immigrants began arriving here during the Gold Rush, around 1849, and this became one of the oldest Chinese neighborhoods in North America. In 1906, an earthquake and fire destroyed almost all of it. Local merchants rebuilt it with pagoda roofs and bright colors, partly to bring in visitors. It worked. Now walk through the gate and head up Grant Avenue, the street straight ahead.
stops.credit: Ilkka Simomaa, CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Up Grant Avenue
stops.text: Keep walking straight up Grant Avenue. Notice the street lamps with little dragons wrapped around them, and the shop signs in Chinese and English. Its old name was Dupont Street, until the city renamed it after President Ulysses Grant. At the next big corner, California Street, look for a red brick church with a clock tower. That's our next stop. Watch out for the cable car tracks as you cross.

stops.name: Old St. Mary's Cathedral
stops.text: This red brick church is Old Saint Mary's. It opened in 1854, when San Francisco was still a rough Gold Rush town, and it was the first cathedral in California. The builders used materials shipped from far away, including granite from China. Look at the clock tower. Under the clock there's a line of text: Son, observe the time and fly from evil. The story goes that it was a warning aimed at the brothels and gambling houses that once filled this corner. In 1906 the great fire gutted the church, but its brick walls stayed standing, and it was rebuilt inside them. You might hear a cable car bell, too. The California Street line runs right past the door. Now continue up Grant Avenue one more block, turn left on Sacramento Street, and take the first right into Waverly Place.

stops.name: Waverly Place and Tin How Temple
stops.text: Welcome to Waverly Place, often called the street of painted balconies. Look up at the upper floors, painted red, green and gold. Many of these buildings belong to family associations and clubs. For generations they helped new arrivals find work, housing and a bit of home in a country that often treated them badly. Find number one twenty five. On its top floor is Tin How Temple, dedicated to Tin Hau, the goddess of the sea, who protects sailors and travelers. The temple dates back to the 1850s, which makes it one of the oldest Chinese temples in the United States. If it's open, you can climb the narrow stairs to a room full of red lanterns and incense. Be respectful, ask before taking photos, and leave a small donation. Then walk to the end of Waverly, turn left on Washington Street, and look for Ross Alley on your right.
stops.credit: Tim Olson, CC BY-SA 2.0, Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Ross Alley
stops.text: This narrow lane is Ross Alley, one of the oldest alleys in the city. In the old days, alleys like this were full of gambling halls and hidden doorways, and Chinatown had a reputation that its residents fought hard to change. Today the main attraction is sweet. Follow the smell of warm vanilla to the Golden Gate Fortune Cookie Factory, a tiny shop where cookies are still folded by hand. Here's a surprise: fortune cookies are not really a tradition in China. Historians believe they came from Japanese bakers and became popular in California restaurants in the early twentieth century. The shop usually asks for a small payment if you take photos, so have some change ready. When you're done, continue to the far end of the alley, turn right on Jackson Street, then right again on Grant Avenue.

stops.name: Back down Grant Avenue
stops.text: You're back on Grant Avenue. Walk one block down to Washington Street and turn left. This part of Grant is where locals shop, with bakeries, herb shops and roast ducks hanging in the windows. If you're hungry, now is a good time for a pork bun or an egg tart. Follow Washington Street downhill for a block. The open plaza on your right is Portsmouth Square.

stops.name: Portsmouth Square
stops.text: Portsmouth Square is where San Francisco began. Before the Gold Rush, this was the plaza of a small village called Yerba Buena, and the water came almost up to this spot. In July 1846, during the war between the United States and Mexico, a United States Navy captain landed here from the ship Portsmouth and raised the American flag. That's where the name comes from. Two years later, the story goes, a merchant named Sam Brannan walked through here waving a bottle of gold dust and shouting about gold in the hills. The rush that followed turned the village into a city almost overnight. Today this is Chinatown's living room. Look for older men playing cards and Chinese chess. When you're ready, walk to the corner of Kearny and Washington Streets, at the top end of the square, and look for a narrow green building.
stops.credit: Unknown authorUnknown author, Public domain, Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Sentinel Building
stops.text: That slim, wedge shaped building with the green copper top is the Sentinel Building, also called Columbus Tower. It was going up when the 1906 earthquake struck, survived the disaster, and was finished soon after. It was built for Abe Ruef, a powerful political boss who later went to prison for bribery. Since the 1970s it has belonged to film director Francis Ford Coppola, the man behind The Godfather. His film company has its offices upstairs, and there's a café on the ground floor. Now look a couple of blocks to the east, and you'll see the tall white Transamerica Pyramid, one of the most famous shapes in the San Francisco skyline. A few steps up Columbus Avenue, turn back, and you can fit both buildings in one classic photo. Now walk up Columbus Avenue, the wide street heading away from downtown on a diagonal.

stops.name: Up Columbus Avenue
stops.text: Keep walking up Columbus Avenue. This diagonal street is the border where Chinatown meets North Beach, the old Italian neighborhood. Soon you'll start to see Italian flags, cafés and restaurants. Keep to the left side of the street. In about a block, just before Broadway, look for a bar called Vesuvio, a small alley, and a bookstore with big windows. That's our next stop.

stops.name: City Lights, Jack Kerouac Alley and Vesuvio
stops.text: You've reached the heart of the Beat Generation. The bookstore is City Lights, founded in 1953 by the poet Lawrence Ferlinghetti and Peter Martin. It was one of the first shops in the country to sell only paperbacks, so ordinary people could afford good books. In 1956, City Lights published Allen Ginsberg's poem Howl. Police arrested the staff for selling an obscene book, and the trial that followed ended in a victory for free speech. The little lane next to it is Jack Kerouac Alley, named after the author of On the Road. Look down for lines of poetry set into the pavement. On the other side of the alley is Vesuvio, a bar the Beat writers loved. The story goes that Kerouac once drank there so long he missed a meeting with the writer Henry Miller. Next, continue up Columbus Avenue, crossing Broadway.

stops.name: Into North Beach
stops.text: You're walking through North Beach. There's no beach here anymore. There once was a shoreline nearby, but it was filled in long ago as the city grew. Italian immigrants made this their neighborhood in the late eighteen hundreds, and you can still smell the espresso. Keep going up Columbus Avenue. When you see a big green park on your right with a white church behind it, you've arrived.

stops.name: Washington Square
stops.text: This is Washington Square, the front lawn of North Beach. Here's a funny detail: it isn't really a square. Columbus Avenue cuts off one corner, so it has five sides. And despite the name, the statue here isn't George Washington. It's Benjamin Franklin, given to the city in the eighteen hundreds. In the early morning, you'll often see neighbors practicing tai chi on the grass, many of them from nearby Chinatown. Later in the day, it fills with people on picnic blankets, dogs and friends meeting for coffee. Take a moment to look around. Chinatown, Italian North Beach and Telegraph Hill all meet around this green. When you're ready, walk across the park toward the big white church with two spires, on Filbert Street.
stops.credit: InSapphoWeTrust from Los Angeles, California, USA, CC BY-SA 2.0, Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Saints Peter and Paul Church
stops.text: This is Saints Peter and Paul Church, finished in 1924. Its two white spires are a landmark you can see from all over the neighborhood. Locals sometimes call it the Italian cathedral, because for a century it has been the spiritual home of North Beach's Italian families. Masses are still held in Italian, along with English and Chinese. The church is famous for one wedding that didn't happen inside. In 1954, baseball star Joe DiMaggio, who grew up in North Beach, married Marilyn Monroe at City Hall. Because he had been divorced, they couldn't marry in the church, but they came here afterwards to take photos on these steps. Now stand with the church behind you and turn left onto Filbert Street. We're heading uphill, toward the tower you can see on top of the hill.
stops.credit: Photo: Mr. Kjetil Ree., CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Up Telegraph Hill
stops.text: Keep climbing Filbert Street. This is Telegraph Hill. In 1849, a signal station on top used a tall pole with moving arms to tell the town when ships were coming through the Golden Gate. Listen for squawking above you. A wild flock of green parrots lives around this hill. Past Kearny Street, Filbert gets too steep for cars and becomes steps. At the top, follow the road and the path up to the tower. Take your time.

stops.name: Coit Tower
stops.text: You made it to Coit Tower, opened in 1933. It was paid for by Lillie Hitchcock Coit, a wealthy and adventurous woman who loved the city's firefighters. When she died, she left part of her fortune to make San Francisco more beautiful. Many people say the tower looks like a fire hose nozzle, but its architects never confirmed that, so take it as a legend. Step inside the ground floor. The walls are covered in murals painted in 1934 by more than twenty five artists, paid by one of the first government art programs of the Great Depression. They show farms, factories, docks and busy city streets. Some scenes were so political they caused an uproar. For a small fee, an elevator takes you to the top for a view of the Bay Bridge, Alcatraz and the Golden Gate Bridge. That's the end of our walk. Thanks for joining me, and enjoy the view.
stops.credit: Dietmar Rabich, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons
